note: Phase 30 of the brief: a bad educational system sees concepts everywhere.
These cases are written BEFORE the concepts they constrain. Each names a surface pattern
that naive recognition would latch onto, and the condition under which the concept does NOT
apply. A concept listed here may not reach stage 'ready' until it carries an engine-tested
counterexample covering its case — tools/run_tests.py enforces that.
fen: null means the position has not been constructed yet; that is itself a tracked gap.

cases.surface_pattern: A knight sits on a central advanced square such as d5.
cases.why_not: An outpost requires that no enemy pawn can challenge the square. If ...c6 or ...e6 is available, the knight is merely visiting.
cases.resolution: Resolved by two independent checks. This base's own Layer 3 detector reports that d5 is NOT a hole for White and returns an empty outpost list, because Black still has the e7 pawn and can play ...e6 - so the system does not make the false positive in the first place. The engine agrees there is nothing to claim: Black stands at +0.74. Note that the question is definitional rather than evaluative, so the detector, not the engine, is the instrument that settles it.

cases.surface_pattern: A rook reaches the opponent's seventh rank.
cases.why_not: The rank matters when it attacks pawns, confines the king, or supports an invasion. A rook on an empty seventh with the enemy king already safe achieves nothing and can be driven away with tempo.
cases.resolution: Resolved. A black rook sits on the seventh with an empty rank to work on and an enemy king that already has luft, and the position is level at -0.04. The two conditions the concept record names as what makes a seventh-rank rook strong are both absent, and the rook is correspondingly worth nothing.

cases.surface_pattern: Two friendly pawns share a file.
cases.why_not: Doubling can open a file for a rook, add central control, and shield a king. Weakness depends on whether they can be attacked and whether they are immobile.
cases.resolution: Resolved twice over. The Ruy Lopez Exchange position, where Black has just accepted doubled c-pawns, evaluates at exactly 0.00. And the cost of inflicting them is measurable from the position one move earlier: 4.Bxc6 is +0.08 where the quiet retreat 4.Ba4 is +0.42, so doubling the opponent's pawns was worth minus 0.34 to the player who did it. The bishop pair and the half-open file pay for the structural damage.

cases.surface_pattern: A bishop sits behind its own pawn chain.
cases.why_not: A bishop hemmed in by pawns on its own colour may still be the key defender of a colour complex, or may become excellent after one pawn break. Mobility, role and prospects matter, not geometry alone.
cases.resolution: Resolved by building the detector the concept needed. lib/features.js now measures both halves of the distinction the record insists on: how many of a side's own pawns share the bishop's colour (structural) and how many squares the bishop actually sees (functional). The matcher requires BOTH before reporting a bad bishop, so Suba's active bad bishop - structurally bad, sees eleven squares - is not reported. The position was found by searching 1576 real positions for the shape rather than constructed to fit. A first version also reported undeveloped bishops on their home squares, which was caught by the existing false-positive regression suite.

cases.surface_pattern: A king has lost its pawn cover or sits in the centre.
cases.why_not: With the attacking pieces traded off, an exposed king is often simply an active king. Exposure matters in proportion to the attacking force that remains.
cases.resolution: Resolved by proof. Both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter whatever - the feature detector reports pawnShield 0 for each - and the tablebase says the position is a draw. King safety is phase-dependent: once the pieces that could punish exposure are gone, the exposed king is not merely safe but is where it should be.

cases.surface_pattern: The queen leaves its starting square in the first few moves.
cases.why_not: The guideline exists because the queen can be harassed with tempo. Where no such harassment exists — the Scandinavian after ...Qa5, or 2.Qh5 lines that have concrete point — the objection does not apply.
cases.resolution: Tested and only partly as expected, which is why it is recorded as partially resolved. The Scandinavian is a sound opening whose queen comes out on move two, so an early queen move must not be reported as an error - that much holds. But it does NOT escape the tempo cost: White is +0.76 here against +0.30 after 1...e5. The correct statement of the false positive is therefore narrower than first written - the pattern must not be flagged as a mistake, but neither should the base claim such openings pay nothing.

cases.surface_pattern: The same piece moves twice inside the first ten moves.
cases.why_not: Concrete gain overrides the guideline: capturing, escaping a threat, or reaching a decisively better square all justify it. This is the brief's own example of principle yielding to tactics.
cases.resolution: Resolved decisively. In the Ruy Lopez after 3...a6, moving the same bishop a SECOND time with 4.Ba4 is the best move at +0.42, against +0.08 for 4.Bxc6 and +0.04 for 4.Bc4. The repeated piece move is not merely acceptable but worth roughly a third of a pawn more than any alternative, in one of the most frequently played positions in chess.

cases.surface_pattern: A pawn has no friendly pawn on either adjacent file.
cases.why_not: An IQP grants central space, two open files and outposts on the squares beside it. It is a dynamic asset in the middlegame and a static liability in the endgame; which dominates depends on how much material remains.
cases.resolution: Resolved. In a standard isolated-queen's-pawn position the side WITH the isolani stands slightly better (+0.14 for White). The isolated pawn buys space, an active bishop and the squares in front of it, and at this stage that is worth marginally more than the structural liability. An isolated pawn must therefore never be reported as a weakness on sight.

cases.surface_pattern: A pawn has no enemy pawn ahead of it on its own or adjacent files.
cases.why_not: A passed pawn that is permanently blockaded by a minor piece is a target rather than an asset, and it can cost tempi to defend.
cases.resolution: PROVEN draw. White has a passed h-pawn, an extra bishop, and the more active king, and cannot win. The pawn is passed and worthless because it is a rook pawn whose promotion square the bishop does not cover. Paired in this base with the identical position with the bishop on the other colour, which is a proven win in 9 - same material, same passed pawn, opposite result.

cases.surface_pattern: A file has no pawns of either colour.
cases.why_not: A file is worth occupying only if it offers entry squares. A file whose seventh and eighth ranks are covered gives a rook nothing but a stare.
cases.resolution: Resolved. A symmetric position with the d-file open and a rook of each colour on it evaluates at +0.02 - dead level, with the best line simply trading the rooks. An open file is not an advantage in itself; it is an advantage only when one side can use it and the other cannot.

cases.surface_pattern: One side is ahead on the standard 1/3/3/5/9 count.
cases.why_not: Piece values are a heuristic for counting, not an evaluation. Compensation in activity, king safety or structure regularly outweighs a pawn or the exchange.
cases.resolution: PROVEN draw with an extra BISHOP AND an extra PAWN. A material count says roughly +4; the truth is a dead draw, because the h-pawn promotes on a square the bishop cannot control and the defending king simply sits in the corner. This is the cleanest available demonstration that counting material is not evaluating a position.

cases.surface_pattern: A move gives check.
cases.why_not: Checks are forcing, not good. A check that drives the king somewhere better, or loses a tempo the attacker needed, is a mistake. This is the commonest beginner misconception in the base.
cases.resolution: PROVEN by the Syzygy tablebase, and controlled in the strongest possible way: this one position contains TWO checks with opposite results. Ra7+ holds the draw; Rg8+ LOSES. The surface pattern 'a check is available' therefore carries no information at all about whether checking is right - in this position it is simultaneously the drawing move and the losing move, depending only on which check. Rh8 and Rf8 also lose, so three of the seventeen legal moves throw away a proven draw.

cases.surface_pattern: A capture or trade is available and the player is materially or positionally ahead.
cases.why_not: Simplification is a method for reducing counterplay, not a rule. Which position you simplify INTO is the whole question, and a trade can convert a won position into a proven draw.
cases.resolution: PROVEN by tablebase, every legal move checked. Rb8 is mate in one. The only capture, Rxh7+, is also a check and is a proven draw, since after Kxh7 only the two kings remain. The one move that simplifies is the one move that throws the game away.

cases.surface_pattern: Few pieces remain and a king has left its back rank, so a material-based phase test calls it an endgame.
cases.why_not: King activation is a claim about a phase in which mating attacks have become unlikely. A material-based phase test can call a position with both queens on an endgame, and centralising into that is an invitation rather than a plan. Shereshevsky separately documents rook endings where centralisation is not merely untimely but wrong.
cases.resolution: Partially resolved and recorded as such. The concept now carries an explicit trap forbidding the recommendation while the opponent has a queen, and the matcher's guard (phase must be endgame AND pawns must be on) is documented as NOT covering this case. A full resolution would mean the matcher itself checking for enemy queens, which is a change to Layer 4 rather than to the record, and is listed as open.

cases.surface_pattern: Each side has exactly one bishop and they run on opposite colours.
cases.why_not: Drawish only when they are nearly the last pieces on the board. With other pieces present the same feature favours the ATTACKER, because each bishop guards a complex the other cannot contest.
cases.resolution: Registered from a near-miss position found by searching 1576 real positions for the surface pattern WITHOUT the concept's condition, then scored by the engine. Level-2 validation: the position was scored, not designed. It confirms the feature is present in real play and, where the score is near level, that the feature is not drowned out. It is not a controlled pair and proves nothing about the concept on its own.

cases.surface_pattern: A king sits on its back rank with no empty escape square.
cases.why_not: The pattern is only dangerous if a rook or queen can reach the back rank. With the heavy pieces gone it costs nothing.
cases.resolution: Registered from a near-miss position found by searching 1576 real positions for the surface pattern WITHOUT the concept's condition, then scored by the engine. Level at -0.24. A king with no luft is only in danger from a piece that can reach the back rank, and with the heavy pieces gone the missing escape square costs nothing. Recorded because the back-rank pattern is one of the easiest features to detect and one of the easiest to over-report.

cases.surface_pattern: One side has both bishops and the other does not.
cases.why_not: The pair's value comes from covering both colours in an OPEN position. In a closed one with no open file, it is worth little and a knight may be the better piece.
cases.resolution: Registered from a near-miss position found by searching 1576 real positions for the surface pattern WITHOUT the concept's condition, then scored by the engine. Level-2 validation: the position was scored, not designed. It confirms the feature is present in real play and, where the score is near level, that the feature is not drowned out. It is not a controlled pair and proves nothing about the concept on its own.

cases.surface_pattern: The fixed geometric facts of the board — colour-boundedness, the knight's colour change, and the fact that a king's diagonal path costs no more than a straight one.
cases.why_not: The rule of the square must be applied with the side to move in hand. This base holds a tablebase-proven pair where the identical position is a draw or a mate in 23 depending only on whose turn it is.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: The conventional numeric values of the pieces, and the properties those numbers compress away.
cases.why_not: Counting material is not evaluating a position. This base holds a PROVEN DRAW a bishop and a pawn up.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: Kings facing each other with one square between them on a rank or file. The side NOT to move has the opposition.
cases.why_not: Kings facing each other is trivially detectable and means nothing outside endgames where king penetration decides.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: A rook pawn whose promotion square is the opposite colour to the bishop's. Bishop and wrong rook pawn cannot win against a king that reaches the corner — the extra material is worth nothing.
cases.why_not: Being in front of the pawn is NOT enough, unlike king-and-pawn endings. The defending king must reach the corner or the square beside it — Mednis gives a position where the same setup wins with White to move and draws with Black to move.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: A file with none of your own pawns on it but one of the opponent's — so your rook looks straight at a pawn that cannot run away sideways.
cases.why_not: A semi-open file is a fact about pawns; whether it produces pressure depends on whether the target is fixed and whether you can attack it more times than it can be defended.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. Quiet and close to balanced at 0.91, which is the combination this base most needs and least often finds: nothing forcing is available and the evaluation is not swamping the feature, so the position is usable as an instance of the concept. What is NOT claimed is that the concept explains the engine's choice of move.

cases.surface_pattern: The drawing method against a rook pawn on the sixth: the defending rook attacks the pawn from the SIDE along the rank, never from behind, with the defending king tucked on g7 or h7.
cases.why_not: It is specialist theory for the ROOK PAWN on the sixth. Applying the side-attack idea to a central pawn does not work.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: What a player receives in return for material given up.
cases.why_not: Being down material with active pieces is not the same as having compensation. The Halloween Gambit position has active pieces and measures 1.75 pawns worse.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. Activity without compensation. 4.Nxe5 gives a knight for a pawn and produces a genuinely mobile centre and gain of time against the black knights, yet evaluates at -1.67 against +0.08 for the best move. Direct evidence that visible activity is not the same thing as adequate compensation, which is the trap this concept most needs guarding against.

cases.surface_pattern: An opening in which material, usually a pawn, is deliberately offered for non-material compensation.
cases.why_not: A pawn offered in the opening is not automatically a gambit with compensation. The Halloween Gambit is measured here at 1.75 pawns worse than the best move.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. A gambit with no adequate compensation, measured. 4.d4 +0.08, 4.Bb5 +0.03, 4.Nxe5 -1.67 - a loss of 1.75 against the best move. The investment of a knight for one pawn is not repaid by the resulting centre. Recorded as a counterexample deliberately: it is what stops this base from treating 'a gambit was played' as evidence that compensation exists.

cases.surface_pattern: Sacrificing one or two pawns to force through a passer the enemy king cannot catch.
cases.why_not: A pawn sacrifice that creates a passer is not a breakthrough unless the passer actually cannot be stopped. The rule of the square decides this and is cheap to check.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. The claim is confirmed exactly and the margin is enormous. The analogous breakthrough 1.b5 evaluates -5.86 and is NOT best; the quiet 1.a5 at -0.46 is. So the same pattern, with the pawns one rank further back, swings from +64.85 (winning by force) to -5.86 (losing) — a difference of over 70 pawns produced by one rank of space, with material and structure held identical. This is the cleanest confirmation in the base

cases.surface_pattern: A square in one's own camp that can no longer be controlled by a pawn, and that the opponent can use.
cases.why_not: Every pawn move creates squares no pawn can guard, so the raw feature fires everywhere. Usability is what makes it reportable.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. Quiet and close to balanced at 0.79, which is the combination this base most needs and least often finds: nothing forcing is available and the evaluation is not swamping the feature, so the position is usable as an instance of the concept. What is NOT claimed is that the concept explains the engine's choice of move.

cases.surface_pattern: A single weakness can usually be defended, because the defender can concentrate every piece on it. Creating a second target far from the first stretches the defence past what it can cover, and somethi
cases.why_not: Two weaknesses that the defending king stands between are not two weaknesses in the operative sense. Measured on the Lasker-Capablanca ending, moving the kings to d3/d6 costs the attacker over half the advantage.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored.

cases.surface_pattern: Bxh7+ against a castled king, followed by Ng5+ and Qh5 — a bishop given to strip the h-pawn and drag the king out.
cases.why_not: The pattern is extremely recognisable, which is exactly why it is played in positions where it does not work. Vukovic's conditions are necessary, NOT sufficient.
cases.resolution: Registered from a recorded counterexample: a position where the concept's surface feature is present and its condition is not, verified mechanically by lib/features.js and then scored. Bxh7+ collapses from BEST at +6.71 to LAST at +3.77 — a swing of 2.94 pawns, and from 1.41 ahead of the field to 1.59 behind it, on one defender of g5. The concept's central precondition is confirmed. HONEST QUALIFICATION: +3.77 still means White is much better, because White is much better in this constructed position for unrelated reasons — the sacrifice throws away most of an advantage rather than losing outright.

cases.surface_pattern: Two rooks stand one behind the other on the d-file — the exact geometry of a battery.
cases.why_not: This record's own trap: "Two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere. Stacked behind their own pawns they combine nothing, and the bare geometry fires on nearly half of all positions." Here the d-file dead-ends at White's own d4 pawn, which is rammed against d5 and cannot move.
cases.resolution: The system does not make the claim: the API reports nothing at all here, because the battery matcher requires the line to arrive at a target and this one arrives at White's own pawn. Stockfish 18 at depth 26 agrees about what the doubled rooks are worth on that file — the position is mate in 5 and the best move is Ra1, which takes the front rook OFF the d-file. The engine's plan is to abandon the battery, which is the strongest possible statement that the geometry was not doing anything.

cases.surface_pattern: A black knight on d5 is attacked by a white bishop. An attacked piece looks hanging.
cases.why_not: This record's own trap: "A defended piece attacked once is not hanging; count both sides of the exchange." The knight is defended by the c6 pawn, and bishop-takes-knight is answered by pawn-takes-bishop.
cases.resolution: PROVEN, not evaluated. The API is silent on hanging-piece, because the matcher asks SEE rather than counting attackers. Syzygy settles what the capture is worth: 5 pieces, draw, dtz 0, and the tablebase's own best move is Bxd5 — the capture is available, is best, and changes nothing, which is exactly what 'attacked once and defended' means. A detector that counted attackers would have called this a hanging knight.

cases.surface_pattern: Both rooks are undefended. An undefended piece is a loose piece.
cases.why_not: This record's own trap: "It only matters when a forcing move can reach it. A loose rook in a locked position is not a weakness." The b-file is stopped by the rammed b4/b5/b6 pawns and no forcing move touches either rook.
cases.resolution: The API does not report loose-piece. The matcher was rewritten for exactly this trap once already — it fired on 66.8% of positions when it counted undefended pieces and on 9.1% once it required a forcing move that survives being forcing. Stockfish 18 at depth 26 evaluates the position at +0.00: two loose rooks and nothing to be done about either. Reporting every undefended piece would flag most positions and teach nothing, which is the trap stated as a firing rate.

cases.surface_pattern: A black pawn on d5 stands directly in front of White's d4 pawn and stops it dead. Something is blockading the pawn.
cases.why_not: This record's own trap: "A pawn stopped by an enemy PAWN is a ram, not a blockade, and no piece is being spent." The whole point of a blockade is the price — a piece is parked in front of the pawn and gives up its freedom to do it. A ram costs nobody anything.
cases.resolution: PROVEN. The API reports nothing: the blockade matcher requires a PIECE on the square in front of the pawn. Syzygy: 4 pieces, draw, dtz 0 — neither pawn ever moves again and no piece was spent to arrange it. The distinction is definitional rather than evaluative, so the detector is the instrument that settles it and the tablebase only confirms that nothing is at stake.

cases.surface_pattern: White's c4 pawn is behind its neighbours on the b- and d-files and cannot advance. That is the surface description of a backward pawn.
cases.why_not: Two of this record's traps fire at once. "A pawn whose advance square is occupied by an enemy pawn is RAMMED. It cannot advance, but not for the reason the concept is about, and the square in front of it is not a hole — an enemy pawn is standing on it." And: "A pawn with no friendly pawn on either adjacent file is ISOLATED, not backward, and reporting both names for one pawn promises the reader a hole in front of it that the isolated case does not create." White's c4 is both.
cases.resolution: The API reports neither backward-pawn nor anything else here. Layer 3 excludes rammed pawns from the backward set and excludes isolated pawns from it by name, both for the reasons quoted above. Stockfish 18 at depth 26: +0.00, best move f4 — the position is dead level and the play is on the other wing, because c4 is not a weakness at all. This is the case that would fool a detector reading 'cannot advance safely' on its own.

cases.surface_pattern: Three white pawns stand abreast on c4, d4 and e4 with no friendly pawns beside them — an advanced, unsupported pawn mass on half-open files.
cases.why_not: Hanging pawns are a PAIR of adjacent pawns on half-open files with no friendly pawns on the flanking files. Three abreast is a phalanx, which is a different structure with different properties: the outer two support the advance of the middle one, and there is no pair to be attacked as a pair.
cases.resolution: This is a REGRESSION CASE, not a hypothetical. The hanging-pawns matcher's `implements` string quoted the flanking-file condition and the code never tested it, so a phalanx of three was reported as a hanging pair; the rate fell from 7.2% to 3.4% when the condition was actually built. The API is now silent here. Syzygy: 5 pieces, WIN for White, dtz 1, mate in 27 — three connected passers on the fourth rank win, which is the opposite of the liability 'hanging pawns' names, and the clearest possible statement that calling this structure by that name would mislead.

cases.surface_pattern: White's rook has the only open file on the board and fourteen legal moves. By any count of available squares it is the most active piece in the position.
cases.why_not: This record's own trap: "Counting available squares is not measuring activity. A piece with many moves that bear on nothing is not active." The a-file leads to an empty corner; there is no entry square, no target on the rank it could switch to, and nothing on the seventh.
cases.resolution: The API reports open-file and does not report piece-activity, which is the correct pair of answers: the file is open and it wins nothing. The matcher stopped counting legal moves for exactly this trap and the rate moved from 44.4% to 33.9%. Stockfish 18 at depth 28: +0.00, and its own first move is Ra6 — the rook goes to the sixth and the position is still dead level. Material is symmetric, so nothing else is carrying the evaluation.

cases.surface_pattern: The black king on g8 has no pawn cover at all — no f-, g- or h-pawn in front of it. An exposed king looks like a king under attack.
cases.why_not: This record's own trap: "An exposed king is not automatically under attack — with the attacking pieces traded off, an exposed king is often just an active one." Both sides have one rook and one pawn. There is nothing left to attack with, and the same is true of White's king.
cases.resolution: The API does not report king-attack. The matcher requires attacking pieces bearing on the king zone rather than an absence of pawn cover, which is what the trap asks for. Stockfish 18 at depth 28: +0.00 in a fully symmetric position — the exposure is mutual and neither side can do anything with it. The related trap on the same record, that the repository's `kingAttack` tag fires on two checks or mate and is a puzzle-classification proxy rather than a definition, is why the matcher does not read that tag here.

cases.surface_pattern: White plays c4-c5, and the pawn on c5 attacks the black pawns on b6 and d6. One piece attacking two enemy units is the definition of a fork, and the detector says so in those words.
cases.why_not: This record's first indicator_against: "The forking piece can simply be captured." Both forked units are pawns, both defend the square the forker stands on, and Black moves first. Also the second: "Both targets are defended and each is worth less than the forker" — here they are worth exactly the same and there are two of them.
cases.resolution: THIS WAS A REAL FALSE POSITIVE and it was reported at HIGH confidence, because a motif tag arrived from findMotifs() with no guard between it and the concept. Syzygy proves the move loses: after c5 the position is 5 pieces, a WIN FOR BLACK, dtz 1, mate in 35, and the tablebase's own best reply is dxc5 — the fork is answered by eating the forker. A guard now implements the record's first indicator_against at the motif-mapping site: if SEE says the piece that just moved can be taken at a profit, the fork is not reported. Rate: fork fell from 16.0% to 11.5% of the 788 shipped puzzles, and the canonical royal fork (Nc7+ forking rook and king) still reports at high.

cases.surface_pattern: After Rxe8, White's rook on e8 attacks the black rook on f8 with the black king behind it on g8. Line piece, enemy unit, more valuable enemy unit, collinear, nothing between — the record's precondition, word for word.
cases.why_not: This record's first indicator_against: "The pinned piece can capture the pinner." The rook on f8 does exactly that, and comes out even. The detector's sentence — "the rook on f8 is pinned to the king behind it and cannot step aside" — is true and misleads, because a reader takes 'cannot step aside' to mean the rook is stuck.
cases.resolution: Reported at HIGH confidence until a guard was written. The geometry is genuinely there, which is why findMotifs() is right to see it; whether it MEANS anything is the concept record's question and the record answers it. The guard reads the pinned square out of the detector's own sentence rather than re-deriving the pin — two implementations of one motif are how the two start to disagree — and suppresses the report when the pinned piece has a legal capture of the pinner that SEE does not punish. It fails open: if the position cannot be rebuilt or the sentence is not in that shape, the motif is reported, because a guard that cannot run has no standing to overrule the detector. Rate: pin fell to 9.0% of the 788 shipped puzzles.

cases.surface_pattern: Rxe8 gives up a rook on a square the enemy rook covers. Material that can be taken, offered anyway — the record's own definition, and SEE returns 500.
cases.why_not: This record's second trap: "An even trade is not a sacrifice." The rook that can be taken was won half a move earlier by the same move.
cases.resolution: A REGRESSION CASE. The matcher's own comment said 'an even trade is not a sacrifice' on the line that tested the size, and the line did not test it: the page's sacrificeSize() answers 'how much can the opponent take on that square now', which is the right question for Bxh7+ and the wrong one for RxR — it returned 500 here and said nothing about the rook the move had just won. Subtracting what the move captured is the whole fix. sacrifice fell from 26.5% to 16.6% of the 788 shipped puzzles, and the Greek-gift shape is untouched, because Bxh7+ nets a bishop minus a pawn and is still a sacrifice.

cases.surface_pattern: c4-c5 advances a pawn into contact with two enemy pawns and opens lines. That is mechanically a break, and it looks like a pawn sacrifice to force something through.
cases.why_not: This record's second trap is a statement about this base rather than about a position: "A break is not a pawn-breakthrough. This base keeps them separate: the breakthrough sacrifices to force a passer, the break challenges a structure." Nothing is forced through here — the pawn is simply eaten.
cases.resolution: The API reports pawn-break at LOW confidence and is silent on pawn-breakthrough, which is the correct pair of answers and the reason the two are separate records with separate matchers. Low is also the honest confidence: this record's first trap says 'whether it is a good one depends on who is placed to use the lines it opens, which the detector cannot see', and Syzygy says this one is not good — Black wins after dxc5, mate in 35. The concept is reported, the judgement is not, and the ceiling on a rule-of-thumb is what keeps the two apart.

cases.surface_pattern: White's queen on d1 and rook on e1 bear down the d- and e-files at d4 and e4. An attack map that counts every line piece credits White with the centre; Black has no piece standing on a central square at all.
cases.why_not: This record's fourth trap: "A rook or queen whose line to a central square runs through one of its own men counts as an attacker and should not be read as a piece fighting for the square." Both white heavy pieces are behind their own d2 and e2 pawns, and both white minors are still at home. Black's bishop on b7 and knight on f6 genuinely bear on the centre from a distance — the record's first trap says the same thing from the other side: "A fianchettoed bishop controls e4 without standing anywhere near it."
cases.resolution: The API reports center-control for BLACK, which is the answer the naive attack map does not give. Material is exactly equal (queen, rook, bishop, knight and two pawns each), so nothing else is carrying the reading. Stockfish 18 at depth 26 scores the position at -4.53 from White's side: Black is winning, on piece placement alone, in a position where White's heavy pieces are the ones aimed at the centre.

cases.surface_pattern: White's pawns on c4, d5 and e4 sit a rank further up the board than Black's on c5, d6 and e5. By any count of squares controlled behind the pawn line, White has a space advantage.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap: "Counting controlled squares is mechanical and over-reports. Space with no entry point wins nothing." Every file is rammed shut and there is no square on Black's half that a white piece can ever occupy.
cases.resolution: The API reports nothing at all here. The space matcher was rewritten for this exact trap and the rate fell from 53.3% to 34.6% of the 788 shipped puzzles when entry squares became a requirement rather than a footnote. Stockfish 18 at depth 26: +0.00, and its line is both kings walking about on the kingside. The extra rank of space is real and worth nothing, which is the trap stated as a number.

cases.surface_pattern: Kd1 in a fully locked position is a quiet, non-committal move that does not lose anything. Quiet moves in blocked positions are the shape prophylaxis and restraint are usually claimed about.
cases.why_not: This record's traps, both of them: "Restraint is not the same as passivity. It reduces the opponent's options; a passive move merely fails to increase yours." And: "Like prophylaxis, it is easy to assert after the fact about any quiet move. Name the advance being prevented." No advance is being prevented — the structure prevents them all by itself, and it did so before the move.
cases.resolution: The API is silent on restraint. The matcher asks whether the move reduces the opponent's safe destinations rather than whether it is quiet, which is the first trap built rather than quoted; and it is move-based, so it cannot be asserted after the fact about the position. This is the case that a keyword rule would fail: every word in the record about quiet moves in blocked positions is present here and the concept is absent.

cases.surface_pattern: Rb1 attacks the black queen on b5 with the rook on b8 directly behind it. More valuable unit in front, less valuable behind, nothing between — the geometry of a skewer, and the detector says so: 'The queen on b5 has to move, and the rook on b8 behind it falls.'
cases.why_not: This record's first indicator_against: "The front unit can capture the skewering piece." The queen is not obliged to move at all; she takes the rook, which is undefended.
cases.resolution: Reported at HIGH confidence until a guard was written. Syzygy settles it without an opinion: after Rb1 the position is a WIN FOR BLACK, dtz 1, mate in 7, and the tablebase's own best move is Qxb1+. The guard is one step wider than the record's wording — it asks whether ANY capture of the skewering piece is profitable rather than only the front unit's — and that is deliberate, because a skewering piece somebody else eats is not a skewer either. skewer fell from 11.4% to 7.6% of the 788 shipped puzzles.

cases.surface_pattern: After Qxf8+, the detector reports 'The rook on c8 is trapped — every square it can reach loses it.' Every square it can reach does lose it.
cases.why_not: This record's second indicator_against: "It has a desperado capture that recovers the material." One of the squares it can reach is f8, where the white queen is standing.
cases.resolution: This is not a constructed position. It is shipped puzzle mi-9f06a55404, and the puzzle's OWN SOLUTION LINE is the refutation of the label: h6f8, c8f8, e7f8q — the second move of the answer is the trapped rook taking the queen. A rook that is lost is trapped; a rook that is lost after eating a queen is a trade. The scan that found it read all 788 shipped puzzles and asked, of every trapped-piece report, whether any capture available to the piece breaks even after recapture: 8 of them do, and all 8 were being reported. The guard implements the condition and trapped-piece fell to 12.9%.

cases.surface_pattern: Nf5 steps out of the c4 rook's line and the detector reports 'Moving the knight uncovers the rook on c4, which now attacks the pawn on f4.' The line really is uncovered and the pawn really is attacked.
cases.why_not: This record's second indicator_against: "The revealed 'attack' hits something defended and not worth taking." The f4 pawn is defended by the knight on d5, so Rxf4 is answered by Nxf4 and the discovery has won a pawn for a rook.
cases.resolution: Shipped puzzle en-f21d044b23, and SEE puts a number on it: taking on f4 scores -400. The move is genuinely strong and the API still says why — Nf5 forks the rook on g7 and the h6 pawn, and that report is untouched. What was wrong was the second label sitting beside the first, telling the reader that a rook had been unleashed onto something. 33 of the 788 shipped puzzles carried a discovered-attack report whose revealed target SEE said was not worth taking; all 33 were at HIGH confidence. A revealed CHECK is never guarded — the detector writes 'now checks the king' for those and the guard does not match that sentence — because a check is worth something whatever SEE says.

cases.surface_pattern: The knight on a1 is beyond argument the worst-placed piece on the board: it has two moves and bears on nothing. Nb3 improves it, the move is quiet, nothing is hanging, and no check is available. Every condition this matcher tests is satisfied.
cases.why_not: This record's second trap: "Improving pieces while the opponent builds an initiative produces individually reasonable moves and a collectively lost position. This is the commonest way the rule is misapplied." And its first indicator_against: "The opponent has a concrete threat that must be met." Black plays Re1 mate.
cases.resolution: Reported as an instance of the rule until a guard was written, and it is the textbook illustration of misapplying it. The matcher already tested the material half of the trap — it refuses when the move leaves a winning capture available — and the sharpest concrete threat there is leaves no material on the floor to detect: the move generator says Black's only mate is e8e1, and Stockfish 18 agrees at depth 20 with #1. The guard is mate in ONE and no further, because whether a threat two moves out 'must be met' is a judgement and this record's third trap is that identifying the worst piece is a judgement this system must not claim to make. A mate the move generator can enumerate is not a judgement. worst-placed-piece fell from 8.4% to 4.1%, and Rubinstein–Salwe 1908 move 20 — the corpus's own annotated instance — still validates.

cases.surface_pattern: White's queen stands directly in front of Black's passed d3 pawn and the pawn cannot advance. That is the record's precondition word for word, and the blockade is real.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap: "A piece standing in front of a pawn is not necessarily blockading it usefully. The test is whether the piece keeps its powers there — a queen on a blockading square is doing a knight's chore." And its first indicator_against: "The blockader is a queen or rook, which is expensive and evictable." A bare report of 'blockade' here tells the reader White has solved a problem.
cases.resolution: THE ANSWER HERE IS THE SENTENCE, NOT A GUARD, and this case exists to pin that down. The concept IS present and suppressing it would be a false negative; what would mislead is reporting it bare. The API says: 'White's queen on d2 stands directly in front of Black's pawn on d3, which has nothing of its own to advance behind and cannot pass it — though a queen is an expensive blockader and can usually be chased off by something cheaper', and attaches two of the record's exceptions as cautions. This is the third of the three answers a stated condition can get — build it, argue on the record that it cannot be built, or say it in the sentence — and it was the right one nine times before this.

cases.surface_pattern: Two kings and one knight each. Neither side has a pawn, a rook or a queen, and neither has more than one minor piece — this record's precondition, word for word.
cases.why_not: The precondition is not the convention. This record's own definition_long names what the convention covers: "K vs K, K+B vs K, K+N vs K, and (in most implementations) K+B vs K+B with bishops on the same colour." Knight against knight is not on that list, and the reason is the one the record gives in the next paragraph about K+N+N vs K: a helpmate exists, so the position is not dead under Art. 5.2.2 and no arbiter declares the game drawn.
cases.resolution: THIS WAS A REAL FALSE POSITIVE and it was reported at the type's ceiling. The matcher tested the precondition per side — no pawn, rook or queen, at most one minor — and that admits two combinations the convention excludes: knight against knight, and bishops of OPPOSITE colours. It now tests the four combinations by name. All four still report: bare kings, a lone bishop, a lone knight, and two bishops of the same colour; and the sentence says which of the four it is, so a reader can check the claim against the board. The distinction matters because this record is filed as TERMINOLOGY rather than as an official rule, precisely so the system does not present a convention as a Law — and a convention that has been widened past what its own definition says is the worst of both.

cases.surface_pattern: King and bishop against king and bishop. One minor piece each, nothing else on the board, and the two bishops can never attack one another.
cases.why_not: Same trap, other half. The convention covers K+B vs K+B only when the bishops are on the SAME colour, because bishops of opposite colours cover disjoint square sets and a helpmate is available. The record's definition_long says 'with bishops on the same colour' and the matcher did not read the qualifier.
cases.resolution: The API is now silent on insufficient-material here and reports `opposite-coloured-bishops` instead, which is the correct concept for this board and was already firing beside the wrong one. The same position with the black bishop on g8 rather than f8 — both bishops light — still reports insufficient-material, which is the controlled comparison: one bishop, one square, and the difference between a convention that applies and one that does not.

cases.surface_pattern: King and bishop against king and bishop with nothing else on the board. Neither side can force mate, which is what a dead position sounds like.
cases.why_not: FIDE 5.2.2 asks whether checkmate can be reached by ANY possible series of legal moves, not whether it can be forced. With bishops on opposite colours a helpmate exists, so the position is not dead — the players may agree a draw, and the arbiter does not end the game.
cases.resolution: The API does not report dead-position here, and the record's own example shows the contrast: K+B vs K, where no series of legal moves reaches mate at all and Syzygy proves the draw over every continuation. The two records are neighbours and the difference between them is exactly this — `insufficient-material` is a software convention and `dead-position` is the Law it approximates, which is why this base keeps them apart and files the first as terminology.

cases.surface_pattern: A white bishop on d3 bears on h7, the black king is castled short behind an untouched h-pawn, and Bxh7+ is available. That is the picture the pattern is famous for.
cases.why_not: This record's third trap, word for word: "Bxh7+ 'looks like' the Greek gift whenever a bishop eyes h7; without the knight and queen in range it is just a lost bishop." White's only knight is on c3 and cannot reach g5. And the fifth indicator_against fires too — a knight covers the kingside: the black knight on f6 guards h7, so the king does not even have to take.
cases.resolution: The API does not report greek-gift, because the matcher asks for Vukovic's three pieces rather than for a bishop pointing at h7. Stockfish 18 settles what the move is worth: the position is 0.00 with a normal move and Bxh7+ scores -3.89, and the refutation is not even Kxh7 - the KNIGHT takes on h7. Nearly four pawns, for the most recognisable sacrifice in chess played one piece short. The record's first trap says the pattern's recognisability is exactly why it gets played where it does not work, and this is that sentence with a number.

cases.surface_pattern: Black's queen has been to c4, c5, h5 and now e5, hitting something every time, and White has answered every time. One side keeps making threats and the other keeps replying: that is what an initiative looks like from outside.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap: "A series of checks is not an initiative. If the opponent's forced replies improve their position, you are helping them." Every one of White's forced answers here — Rxd6, Rad1, Ne3, Nd4, Nc4 — centralises a piece.
cases.resolution: Reti-Capablanca, New York 1924, move 27, and it is a world champion making the mistake. Keene: 'Capablanca is really doing his utmost on the fourth rank with his strongest piece, but the queen is no match for White's heavily centralised knights and rooks. Black had to try an exchange sacrifice and play 27...Rxe3!' The API reports weak-square and open-file here and does not report initiative — correctly, and for a reason the record states as its third trap: the initiative is a property of the SEQUENCE and is not detectable from the board at all. Corpus entry `reti-capablanca-1924-27Qe5-initiative-negative`.

cases.surface_pattern: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 5.d4 — the Halloween Gambit. White has given a knight for a pawn and has a big centre with tempo, every piece pointing forward, and Black's knight about to be chased twice.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap names this exact opening: "Being down material with active pieces is not the same as having compensation. The Halloween Gambit position has active pieces and measures 1.75 pawns worse."
cases.resolution: The API does not report compensation here. Stockfish 18 at depth 22 says +1.71 from Black's side, which is the record's own figure re-measured independently and arriving within four centipawns of it. The activity is real; the compensation is not. Note what the API DOES report — center-control for White — which is true and is the thing that makes the position look compensated.

cases.surface_pattern: Kd1 in a locked position: a quiet, non-committal move that loses nothing and can be described afterwards as restraining Black's plans.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap: "Any quiet move can be called prophylactic after the fact. The claim requires naming the specific idea prevented — if you cannot name it, the move was just quiet." Nothing is prevented here; the structure prevents everything by itself, and did so before the move.
cases.resolution: The API reports nothing at all here — not prophylaxis, not restraint, not anything. That is the correct answer and it is the one a keyword rule would fail: every word in the record about quiet moves in blocked positions is true of this position, and the concept is absent. This record's third trap is why there is no matcher for it: prophylaxis is a property of what a move DENIES, which requires knowing what the opponent intended, and this base does not guess at intentions.

cases.surface_pattern: Both rooks are undefended in a position where the phrase 'loose pieces drop off' would be quoted without a second thought.
cases.why_not: This record's first indicator_against: "Closed position where no forcing move reaches the loose piece." The b-file is stopped by rammed pawns and no forcing move touches either rook. And its first trap: "A piece being undefended is not a mistake, and calling it one teaches a habit of pointless defending."
cases.resolution: The API reports neither lpdo nor loose-piece here. The `loose-piece` matcher was rewritten for exactly this and fell from 66.8% of shipped positions to 9.1% when it began requiring a forcing move that survives being forcing; `lpdo` is the aphorism about the same fact and inherits the discipline. Stockfish 18: +0.00. Two loose rooks and nothing to be done about either. The record's second trap is worth reading beside this: a ChessBase reader showed that the article which coined the phrase had chosen an example that was not an instance of it.

cases.surface_pattern: Two rooks and a king, all developed, none in each other's way, each with an open file. Nothing is badly placed and a reader looking for a name would reach for coordination.
cases.why_not: This record's second indicator_against: "Pieces on opposite wings with unrelated purposes." And its second trap: "Individually well-placed pieces are not the same as coordinated pieces, and this is exactly the distinction the concept exists to make."
cases.resolution: The API reports open-file and piece-activity and does not report coordination, which is the right set of three answers. This record's first trap is the reason it has no matcher at all: "This is the concept most easily misused as a label for any quiet move whose point is not understood. It must never be the default explanation when nothing else fits" — so the concept is deliberately unreachable from the board, and this case exists to hold that decision in place rather than to test a guard.

cases.surface_pattern: After Rxd5 the black king sits behind three unmoved pawns with no luft, and a rook landing on the eighth rank would be mate. The detector verifies that with the move generator rather than assuming it.
cases.why_not: This record's second indicator_against: "A second defender covers the back rank." The rook on d8 covers it, and Black is to move — the mate exists only if White is handed a free move, which is exactly how the detector asks the question.
cases.resolution: THE ANSWER IS THE SENTENCE, and one sentence was wrong. The detector's own text is conditional and correct — 'the king is shut in on its own back rank by its own pieces, and a rook or queen landing there is mate' — and so are by_depth.normal and by_depth.deep. But `explanations.by_level.intermediate` said 'the back rank is not adequately defended', which is false here: it is defended, by the rook that is about to capture. That level now reads 'unless a defender covers it, and the standing weakness is that whatever covers it can then be deflected', which is both true of this position and the actual content of the concept. The concept is still reported, correctly: the back-rank weakness is real and permanent, and the deflection theme is what it is for.

cases.surface_pattern: King, bishop and rook-pawn against a bare king in the corner. This is the picture of the most famous fortress in chess: the defender sits on h8 and cannot be dislodged.
cases.why_not: The bishop is the WRONG colour for that fortress, or rather the right one. The drawn version needs a bishop that does not control the queening square; here the bishop is dark-squared and h8 is dark, so the defending king can be driven out and the pawn queens.
cases.resolution: PROVEN, not evaluated. The API does not report a fortress here. Syzygy: 4 pieces, WIN, dtz 1, mate in 9, best move Kg6+. Read against this record's own positive example, which is the SAME material with the bishop on the other colour and is a proven draw at dtz 0 — one bishop, two colours, mate in nine and a dead draw. That pair is why a fortress claim in this base is only ever made with a proof behind it: the two positions are indistinguishable to any test that counts material.

cases.surface_pattern: The white king stands on g6, directly in front of and beside its own passed pawn, with the black king shut in the corner. For any other pawn on the board that square is a key square and the position is winning.
cases.why_not: A rook pawn has no key squares in the ordinary sense, because the defending king cannot be driven off the queening square — there is no room on the other side of the pawn to be driven towards.
cases.resolution: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, and the tablebase's own best move is h6 — which leads nowhere. The API does not report key-square. This is the case that catches a detector built on 'the king is in front of the pawn': the geometry is identical to the winning case and the file is the whole difference. Compare `wrong-rook-pawn`, which is the same fact stated about the bishop instead of the king.

cases.surface_pattern: Kings in direct opposition in a king-and-pawn ending, Black to move and every king move giving ground. That is what zugzwang looks like.
cases.why_not: Zugzwang requires that having to move is what hurts, and here it is not: White has a spare pawn on h3 and wins whether it is Black's move or his own. There is no mutual obligation, so nobody is in zugzwang — Black is simply lost.
cases.resolution: PROVEN both ways, which is what settles it: with Black to move the position is a loss in 26, and with WHITE to move it is a win in 25 and the tablebase's own best move is h4 — the spare tempo. The API does not report zugzwang. It does report `opposition` at high confidence, and that is correct and worth noticing: the opposition is present and it is not what decides. Remove the h-pawn and the same board becomes this base's strictest controlled pair, where the side to move loses and the side not to move draws.

cases.surface_pattern: Neither side has an a-pawn, so a6 and a3 are squares no pawn can ever attack — the definition of a hole, satisfied twice on the same board.
cases.why_not: This record's fourth indicator_against: "The square is on the edge or deep in the opponent's own half, where occupying it achieves nothing." And its first trap: "Every pawn move creates squares no pawn can guard. Most of them are irrelevant."
cases.resolution: The API reports `outpost` and `weak-square` for d5 and says nothing about a6 or a3. That is the correct set of answers, and the interesting half is what is NOT reported: a naive hole detector finds three holes here and two of them are noise. The record's own trap is that most holes are irrelevant, and this position is that trap with a count attached.

cases.surface_pattern: Black has played ...g6 and fianchettoed, so f6 and h6 are permanently weak on the dark squares and no black pawn will ever cover them again. This is the most-taught hole in the openings.
cases.why_not: This record's third trap, in full: "Fianchetto structures leave permanent holes on the long-diagonal colour complex that are nonetheless well covered by the bishop; the hole is real, the weakness is not." The bishop on g7 covers the complex it created.
cases.resolution: The API does not report a hole here. This is the same trap that `weak-square` was tightened against — the fianchetto guard lives in reachableHoles() in Layer 3 and is quoted in a comment there — and `hole` inherits it, because both concepts read the same Layer 3 output. The case exists so that inheritance is pinned down rather than assumed: a guard in a shared function protects whoever happens to call it, and nothing in the code says which concepts those are.

cases.surface_pattern: White's king is on e1, both rooks are on their home squares, nothing stands between them, and the FEN grants both rights. Every visible condition for castling is met.
cases.why_not: This record's third indicator_against: "The crossed or destination square is attacked." The black bishop on b5 covers f1, so O-O would take the king through check.
cases.resolution: Settled by the instrument that IS the rule. This base's move generator produces exactly one castling move here, e1c1, and does not produce e1g1; on the same board with the bishop removed it produces both. All three of this record's indicators_against are the Law rather than heuristics, and legalMoves() in blind-chess.html is the only implementation of it this repository has or should have — the same function that decides castling in a game decides it here. There is nothing for a matcher to guard, and adding one would be a second implementation of a rule that already has one.

cases.surface_pattern: A white pawn on e5 stands beside a black pawn on d5. That is the picture of an en-passant capture and it is the position the rule is drawn in every textbook.
cases.why_not: This record's only indicator_against: "Any other move has intervened since the two-square advance." The right to capture lasts exactly one move, and the FEN records that in one field.
cases.resolution: Two FENs, one character apart. With the en-passant field set to `-`, this base's move generator produces six legal moves and none of them is exd6. With the field set to `d6` it produces seven, and the seventh is exd6. The board is identical in both. This is the sharpest available illustration of the `notation` record's third trap — 'a FEN without the castling, en passant and clock fields is not a position, it is a picture of one' — and of why en-passant cannot be read off a diagram.

cases.surface_pattern: 'Nd2' looks like a complete move. There is a knight, there is a square, the square is empty and reachable.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap: "SAN is contextual: the same text means different moves in different positions, and disambiguation depends on what else is on the board." Two knights reach d2 here, so 'Nd2' names two moves and therefore none.
cases.resolution: This base's own toSAN() writes the three moves to d2 as Nfd2, Nbd2 and Kd2 — it disambiguates by file because it must, and it is the same function the game writes its move list with. The case exists because the failure here is silent: a reader, a database or a converted quotation that drops the disambiguating letter produces text that looks like notation and denotes nothing, and no error is raised anywhere.

cases.surface_pattern: The halfmove clock reads 149. One more move with no capture and no pawn move and the arbiter ends the game as a draw, whatever the position looks like.
cases.why_not: This record's only indicator_against: "The final move delivers checkmate — mate takes precedence." The move that reaches 150 is Ra8, and it is mate.
cases.resolution: The move generator settles it: the only mate in one here is a1a8, and it is a rook move that captures nothing and moves no pawn, so it is precisely the move that would otherwise trigger the rule. FIDE 9.6.2 makes mate take precedence, and this base does not need a guard for that because the rule and the exception are decided by the same function — a position with no legal moves and the king in check is checkmate before anything else is asked about it.

cases.surface_pattern: The halfmove clock reads 96. Two more moves each and either side may claim a draw.
cases.why_not: This record's only indicator_against: "Any capture or pawn move in that span resets the counter." White is in check and has exactly one legal move, Kxg2, which is a capture. The counter goes back to zero on the next ply and the claim never becomes available.
cases.resolution: The move generator produces one legal move, h1g2, and it is a capture. The matcher does report fifty-move-rule here — correctly, because what it says is '96 ply have passed with no capture and no pawn move; at 100 either side may claim a draw', which is true and is a statement about the count rather than a prediction. This case is registered to hold that distinction in place: the concept is about a counter, the counter is at 96, and whether it ever reaches 100 is a question about the game and not about the position. A matcher that tried to predict it would be guessing.

cases.surface_pattern: White's bishop has gone b5 then a4: the same piece moved twice in the opening, and Black has developed a piece in between. By the rule as it is usually taught, White has lost a tempo.
cases.why_not: This record's third trap, and it is the one the record itself says is registered: "Treating 'moved the same piece twice' as automatically a lost tempo. This is a registered false-positive case: a capture, an escape, or a decisively better square are all reasons to move it again." Here it is an escape — Black played ...a6 to attack the bishop — and the tempo Black spent attacking it is the same tempo White spent retreating.
cases.resolution: WRITTEN BECAUSE THE RECORD CLAIMED IT ALREADY EXISTED. The `tempo` record said 'this is a registered false-positive case' and no case with that concept was in this file — a claim the file did not back, which is the same defect class as an `implements` string claiming what the code does not do. A test now asserts that any record using that phrase has a case. The position is the Ruy Lopez after 4.Ba4, the most-played opening in the history of the game; Stockfish 18 at depth 22 says -0.43 from Black's side, an ordinary opening edge for White. The API reports nothing about tempo here, correctly: this base has no tempo matcher, because counting tempi requires knowing whether the forced reply was one the opponent wanted, and that is not on the board.

cases.surface_pattern: A rook-and-pawn ending with the defending rook NOT on its third rank and the attacking king already escorting the pawn. This is what a failed Philidor defence should look like.
cases.why_not: The Philidor defence has a condition — the rook holds the third rank until the pawn reaches the sixth, and then checks from behind. A position where the defender has not set up should be lost, and showing that is what a counterexample here would do.
cases.status_note: OPEN. Four constructions have been tried and Syzygy answered DRAW to every one of them: R7/8/8/8/4k3/4p3/1r6/4K3 b, 8/8/8/4k3/4p3/8/R7/1r2K3 w, 8/8/8/4k3/4p3/4K3/R7/1r6 w and the position on this line, all dtz 0. With the pawn on the fourth rank the defence holds from almost anywhere, which is itself the finding: the method is far more robust than the textbook statement of it, and the position that would show it failing needs the pawn further advanced AND the defending rook misplaced AND the defending king cut off, which is three conditions rather than one.
cases.resolution: NOT RESOLVED, and recorded so. This case is deliberately left open rather than filled with a position that does not show what it claims. tools/depth_report.py counts only resolved and partially-resolved cases towards a concept's false-positive coverage, so nothing in this base's score moves because this exists - it is here to keep a known gap visible, which is the whole reason the file has a status field.

cases.surface_pattern: Nd6+ attacks the king on e8 and the pawn on c7 — one knight, two enemy units, with check. That is the geometry of a royal fork.
cases.why_not: This record's own paired example makes the distinction: with a bishop on b7 the same knight on the same square forks king and bishop, and with b7 empty it checks and attacks a defended pawn. "A fork needs two things worth taking", and a pawn defended by the king it is forking is not one of them.
cases.resolution: PROVEN. The API does not report a fork, and Syzygy says the position is a DRAW at dtz 0 whose best move is Nxa7 — a different capture entirely. The controlled pair on this record is one man apart: put a bishop on b7 and the same move becomes a genuine fork, and the tablebase still says draw, because the fork wins a bishop and knight-and-king against king-and-two-pawns is drawn. Two positions, one piece of difference, and the RESULT is the same in both — which is the point of the pair. It isolates whether the fork is there, not who is winning.

cases.surface_pattern: A knight on g5, a black king on h8, a rook on g8 boxing it in — the smothered-mate picture, and Nf7+ is available.
cases.why_not: This record's first indicator_against: "A flight square is empty or can be vacated." One pawn stands on h6 instead of h7, so after Nf7+ the king goes to h7.
cases.resolution: PROVEN, and the proof is the sharpest pair in this base. With the pawn on h7 the same knight move is mate in ONE by tablebase. With it on h6 the same move leaves White PROVEN LOST — dtz -4, mate in 38 against — because the knight has walked into a corner it cannot leave. One pawn, one square, and the difference between mate in one and mate in thirty-eight the other way. The API reports neither smothered-mate nor checkmate here.

cases.surface_pattern: The white rook on d1, the black bishop on d6, the black rook on d7 and the black queen on d8 are all on the d-file with nothing else between them. A line piece acting through another piece towards something more valuable is the definition of an x-ray.
cases.why_not: This record's first indicator_against: "A second blocker sits further along the line." The precondition is a line piece, ONE intervening unit and a further square of interest; here there are two intervening units, so the rook acts through nothing — the pressure stops at the bishop.
cases.resolution: The API does not report x-ray. The distinction is worth stating because it is arithmetical rather than positional: one blocker is an x-ray, two is a queue, and the difference is a count that a reader looking at a file of pieces will not naturally make. This record's positive example is the DEFENSIVE form of the same geometry with exactly one blocker, tablebase-proven, and the two sit side by side for that reason.

cases.surface_pattern: Bxd5 captures a defended pawn and removes a unit that was guarding it. Capturing what defends the target is the concept's second precondition, word for word.
cases.why_not: The first precondition is that the target IS defended after the removal, and here the d5 pawn has two defenders — the pawns on c6 and e6. Taking one leaves the other, so nothing has been removed in the sense the concept means: the whole idea is that the target becomes takeable, and it does not.
cases.resolution: The API does not report removing-the-defender. This record's positive example is the same shape with ONE defender — a knight on f6 guarding d5, a bishop on g5 to take it, +4.81 — and the two differ by a single pawn. The concept is a counting claim before it is a tactical one, which is why the positive example's note says what makes it clean: the bishop's capture wins nothing by itself, so the move only makes sense as removal of a guard.

cases.surface_pattern: The pawn on d5 is defended by the bishop on e4 and the queen on d3 with a rook behind her — three units aimed at one square, which is Nimzowitsch's picture of an overprotected strong point.
cases.why_not: This record's second trap: "This is the idea most likely to license bad advice. Do not report it unless the overprotecting pieces are demonstrably well placed for other reasons as well." And its second indicator_against: "The point is not under any real pressure." Nothing attacks d5 at all.
cases.resolution: The API reports battery, center-control and passed-pawn here and does not report overprotection. That is the right set: the geometry really is a battery, the pawn really is passed, and the CLAIM that the extra defence is worthwhile is the one thing nobody can read off the board. This record's first trap says so in as many words — 'counting defenders is mechanical and says nothing' — and it is why there is no matcher.

cases.surface_pattern: A white pawn one square from queening, the white king in front of it, the black king cut off, and a black rook checking from behind. That is the Lucena position, and the technique is one of the first things any player is taught.
cases.why_not: The Lucena method needs a file on each side of the pawn to build the bridge on, and a rook pawn has only one. Nothing else about this position differs from the winning version - the same pieces, the same relative geometry, one file across.
cases.resolution: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, best move Ra1, and Stockfish agrees at 0.00. Read against this record's own positive example, which is the same setup with a knight pawn and is a PROVEN WIN in 41. The API does not report lucena-position here. What makes the pair worth having is that no test counting material, files, ranks or piece relationships can separate the two: the difference is the letter of the file, and it is worth the whole game.

cases.surface_pattern: A white knight sits on d5, a square no black pawn can ever attack - the c-pawn is gone and the e5 pawn captures towards d4 and f4. The first precondition holds in full.
cases.why_not: The second precondition does not: no friendly pawn defends the square. White's pawn is on e3 rather than e4, so the knight is held by the queen on d1 and attacked by the queen on d8. This record's own indicator_against is "The square can only be held by pieces, not pawns", and its own sentence for the case is that such a square is a liability wearing a good square's clothes.
cases.resolution: The API reports neither strong-square nor outpost nor weak-square here; with the pawn on e4 instead of e3 it reports outpost for White and weak-square for Black. Stockfish 18 at depth 22 puts the difference at 47 centipawns - -0.17 here against +0.30 there - and its own first move in this position is e3-e4, which is to say it plays the move that turns this half of the pair into the other half. That is a stronger statement about what the pawn is worth than either evaluation is.

cases.surface_pattern: A wing pawn advance against an enemy pawn group, aiming to create a weakness. That is the plan a minority attack executes, and the word 'minority' is the part readers drop.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap: "Advancing pawns on the wing where you have fewer is only right in this specific structure. Elsewhere it is simply weakening." White has THREE queenside pawns against Black's two. Advancing there is a majority attack, whose point is a passed pawn, and this record's third trap draws the line explicitly: "The goal is a fixed weakness, not space and not a passed pawn."
cases.resolution: The API reports nothing here, which is correct and is the whole content of the case: the concept turns on a COUNT that is trivial to make and trivial to skip. Three against two is a majority and two against three is a minority, and the same pawn move means opposite things in the two cases. This base has no minority-attack matcher, and this position is one reason - the plan is named by the count AND by the structure, and the record's second trap adds a third condition on top of both.

cases.surface_pattern: White's rook can check the black king along the eighth rank and follow it about indefinitely. A stream of checks the defender can never escape is what a perpetual is.
cases.why_not: Two of this record's conditions fire at once. The first trap: "A series of checks that merely delays the end is not a perpetual. The test is whether the position REPEATS, not whether checks are available." And the third indicator_against: "The checking side is BETTER, in which case the perpetual is a failure, not a resource." White is a whole rook up.
cases.resolution: The API does not report perpetual-check. Stockfish 18 at depth 26 says +56.95: taking a draw by repetition here would be one of the worst decisions available on the board. This record's third trap is the one that matters most and it is about the reader rather than the detector - 'reporting a perpetual as a good outcome for the side that was winning inverts the meaning entirely' - which is why the concept must be reported with the side named or not at all.

cases.surface_pattern: Two kings and a knight in an endgame, with the side to move wanting to hand the move back. Triangulation is the standard way to do that, and the knight looks like a piece with spare moves to make.
cases.why_not: A knight cannot lose a single tempo: every knight move changes the colour of the square it stands on, so returning to the same square always takes an even number of moves. Triangulation is precisely the technique of reaching the same position with the OTHER side to move, and a knight can never contribute one.
cases.resolution: The API does not report triangulation. Syzygy: 3 pieces, draw, dtz 0 — the position is drawn whoever moves, so there is no tempo worth losing in it either. The geometric fact is the interesting half and it is not evaluative at all: a king triangulates because it can reach a square in two moves or three, and a knight's parity forbids the equivalent. This is why the technique belongs to king-and-pawn endings and to bishops, and why a knight ending is the standard example of a position where zugzwang cannot be manufactured.

cases.surface_pattern: White has advanced four pawns to c4, d4, e5 and f4 against a King's Indian setup. Four abreast rolling at the enemy king is the picture the phrase describes.
cases.why_not: This concept's condition is that pieces follow into the lines the pawns open. Letelier's every piece is at home except one bishop; the annotation names both the concept and the reason it fails — "his opponent decided to launch an early pawn storm against Black's King's Indian and delay his development. When central pawns are not supported by pieces, they can become an easy target for the opponent."
cases.resolution: Letelier-Fischer, Leipzig Olympiad 1960, and Fischer won in twenty-three moves. The API reports center-control for White here and does not report a pawn storm; Stockfish 18 at depth 24 says -0.10, level, with the storm complete and nothing gained. The same position is this record's counterexample and `historical-principles`' positive example — a rule caught losing its condition — which is the same fact filed under the rule and under its history.

cases.surface_pattern: Rxd5 hands over a rook for a knight. That is the material transaction the concept names, and it is available and correct.
cases.why_not: This record's MAIN trap, in its own words: "a rook given up inside a forced mating line is a mating sacrifice, not a positional exchange sacrifice, even though the material given is identical." The point of Rxd5 is not a long-term asset — it is that the rook on d8 cannot recapture, because Re8 would then be mate.
cases.resolution: The API does not report exchange-sacrifice. It reports back-rank-mate, hanging-piece and sacrifice, which between them describe what is actually happening. Stockfish 18 at depth 22 says +6.73 and its own line is Rxd5 followed by ...Rb8 — Black DECLINES the recapture and is simply a knight down. This position is `overloading`'s positive example, and the two records reading the same board differently is the point: what the exchange record would have to claim is that a rook was invested in a position, and what happened is that a rook was never taken.

cases.surface_pattern: A pawn one square from queening, the king in front of it, the enemy rook checking from behind, and a rook ready to come to the fourth rank. Every ingredient of the bridge is on the board.
cases.why_not: The bridge is built by putting the rook on the fourth rank and then interposing it on the file BESIDE the pawn once the king walks out. A rook pawn has no file on one side, so there is nowhere to interpose and nowhere for the king to walk to.
cases.resolution: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0. This record's positive example is the same position with a knight pawn and is a PROVEN WIN in 41 whose first move is Rd1+ — the check that starts the bridge. The two boards differ by the file of one pawn and the file of one rook. A technique record is a claim that a position is winnable BY A METHOD, so the pair it needs is one where the method is unavailable rather than one where the material is different, and this is that pair.

cases.surface_pattern: A minor-piece ending with no pawns on the queenside at all. 'Bishops are better in the endgame' is the first thing most players learn, and there is nothing here to complicate it.
cases.why_not: This record's second trap says the opposite is true in this exact structure: "Pawns on one side only REVERSES the usual open-position reasoning — the knight is stronger there, which surprises people who have learnt 'bishops are better in the endgame'." With one wing to defend, the bishop's range buys nothing and the knight's ability to reach both colours buys everything.
cases.resolution: The API does not assert that either piece is better here, and this record has no matcher for exactly the reason its first trap gives: "There is no default answer. Asserting the bishop is better without naming the structural reason is exactly the claim GM Studer says has no evidence behind it." Stockfish 18 at depth 24 says 0.00 — dead level, which is the honest reading and is itself the evidence against the folk rule: if bishops were simply better in endgames, three pawns each and a bishop against a knight would not evaluate to zero.

cases.surface_pattern: Black has two checks available with the same rook. A check is the most forcing move there is, and the rule says to look at the forcing moves first.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap, and the record names this exact position: "Forcing is not the same as good, and this is the trap that matters. This base holds a proven position in which one check draws and another loses." The Vancura position. ...Rd6+ holds; ...Rf4+ loses.
cases.resolution: PROVEN, both of them, and this is the claim the record has been making in prose. After ...Rd6+ the position is still a DRAW at dtz 0. After ...Rf4+ it is a WIN FOR WHITE, dtz 21, mate in 67. Two checks by one rook from one square, one holding and one losing by force, and nothing about their forcing-ness distinguishes them. The rule is about search ORDER and not about move choice, which is this record's second trap, and a position where the two most forcing moves available differ by sixty-seven moves of result is the sharpest way to say it.

cases.surface_pattern: After 1.e4 e5 2.Qh5 the white queen stands on the fifth rank attacking two things at once, further advanced than any other piece on the board.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap: "An advanced queen is not an active queen. It is often a queen about to be chased, and the chasing moves develop the opponent."
cases.resolution: The API does not report queen-activity.
