What makes this case worth registering is the SIZE of the effect rather than its direction: the engine says +0.39 for White, an ordinary opening edge, and this base has measured the early-queen cost at about 0.68 in the standard case. The move is not a blunder. This record's second trap says so itself — 'real, and much smaller than the usual teaching tone' — and the case exists to keep the base from adopting the tone.

cases.surface_pattern: Two diagrams, piece for piece identical: kings on e1 and e8, rooks on a1, h1, a8 and h8, nothing else on the board. Any comparison that reads the squares alone calls them the same position.
cases.why_not: This record's second trap: "Castling rights are invisible on the board but are part of the position. Two arrangements that look identical are not transpositions if one side has lost the right to castle."
cases.resolution: Settled by counting moves. With the rights present this base's move generator produces 26 legal moves including e1g1 and e1c1; with them absent it produces 24 and no castling. Same men, same squares, two legal positions, and the difference is in a FEN field rather than on the board. The `notation` record's third trap is the same fact from the other side — 'a FEN without the castling, en passant and clock fields is not a position, it is a picture of one' — and `en-passant`'s registered case is the third member of that family.

cases.surface_pattern: White is much worse and retreats a piece to a square where it defends. Retreating and consolidating is what a worse position seems to call for.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap: "Defence is not passivity. Recommending a passive move because a position is worse is the commonest defensive error, not a defensive principle." Speelman's account of the game says exactly this happened — Adams, 'seeing no good way to continue his attack, panicked and blundered' with 22.Nb3.
cases.resolution: Adams-Kasparov, Linares 2005, and the two candidate moves are 234 centipawns apart: 22.Be3, the move Speelman says was best and this record's positive example, scores -1.91, and the retreat 22.Nb3 that was played scores -4.25. Both are bad. That is the point of the pair — the choice is not between saving the game and losing it, it is between the least bad move and a worse one, and the passive move is the worse one. The API reports nothing about defensive principles either way, because the concept has no matcher: what makes a move defensive is what it prevents, and this base does not read intentions.

cases.surface_pattern: Rxd5 gives up a rook for a knight and gets no material back. Material invested for something other than material is what a positional sacrifice is.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap: "Calling any unclear sacrifice positional. If the point is an attack, it is not a positional sacrifice." Nothing is invested here at all — the rook cannot be recaptured, because Rxd5 would allow Re8 mate. The 'compensation' is a mate in two.
cases.resolution: The API does not report positional-sacrifice. It reports back-rank-mate, hanging-piece and sacrifice, and the engine's line — Rxd5 followed by ...Rb8 rather than ...Rxd5 — shows what the move actually is: Black declines and is simply a knight down, +6.73. This record's second trap is the reason it has no matcher: 'asserting compensation that cannot be named. Positional compensation with no named asset is the vaguest claim in chess writing and must not be produced by this system.' The same position is `exchange-sacrifice`'s registered case and `overloading`'s positive example — three records reading one board, and only one of them is entitled to it.

cases.surface_pattern: A forced sequence of checks running nineteen moves to mate, with the defender's replies determined throughout. A long forcing line ending in mate is what most players mean by a combination.
cases.why_not: This record's second trap: "A forcing sequence without a sacrifice is a manoeuvre on Botvinnik's account and a combination on Romanovsky's. Reporting it either way takes a side in a live disagreement." Nothing is sacrificed here at any point.
cases.resolution: The API reports double-check and does not report a combination. Syzygy: PROVEN WIN, dtz 17, mate in 19 — so the sequence really is forced and really does reach a goal, which is the third trap's requirement ('length and forcing-ness do not make a combination; there has to be a goal it reaches'). What it does not have is a sacrifice, and this record's FIRST trap forbids the system from deciding whether that matters: 'whether a sacrifice is REQUIRED is contested by named authorities, so this system must not assert either version as the definition.' Not reporting is the only answer that does not take a side.

cases.surface_pattern: Black has a passed pawn on d3, one square from the second rank. A passed pawn is the textbook dynamic asset: it must be pushed, and its value expires if it is not.
cases.why_not: This record's first trap: "The classification is not a property of the feature alone. A passed pawn is static if it can be held and dynamic if it must run now." This one is held permanently, by a queen standing directly in front of it, and it will never move again.
cases.resolution: The API reports blockade and passed-pawn here and says nothing about static or dynamic, which is the correct pair of answers: both features are present and the CLASSIFICATION is a claim about whether the advantage expires, which is a claim about the future. Stockfish 18 at depth 26 says mate in 10 for White — the pawn is not merely held, it is irrelevant. This record's second trap is the reason there is no matcher: 'dynamic is often used loosely to mean sharp. Here it means specifically that the advantage expires', and nothing on a board says when.

cases.surface_pattern: Kd1 in a fully locked position. Any quiet move can be described afterwards as part of a plan — improving the king, preparing to bring it to the queenside, waiting for the opponent to commit.
cases.why_not: A plan is a sequence with a goal, and this position has no goal available to anybody: every file is rammed shut and no piece can enter. Describing the move as planful names an intention the board does not contain.
cases.resolution: The API reports nothing at all here — not planning, not prophylaxis, not restraint — and the engine says 0.00 with both kings walking about on the kingside. The three concepts share this position as a registered case for the same reason: each is a claim about what a move is FOR, and this base reports what is on the board. A position where every word of three records is true and none of the three concepts is present is the sharpest available test of that discipline.

cases.surface_pattern: Bxb7+ steps the bishop off the d-file, the queen on d4 checks the king on d8 through the gap, and the bishop takes a pawn on the way. That is a discovered check and the detector reports the discovery.
cases.why_not: This record's first indicator_against: "The check is easily blocked or the checking piece captured." The whole value of a DISCOVERED check over an ordinary one is that the reply must answer the check, which frees the moving piece to do anything. Here Black answers with ...Nd7, blocking, and keeps every other option.
cases.resolution: Shipped puzzle mi-f2e1be14e7, and the useful part is that the MOVE IS EXCELLENT: Stockfish 18 says +4.67 at depth 22, first choice by nearly four pawns. The API reports `discovered-attack` here and refuses `discovered-check`, which is the right pair of answers - the discovery is real and the claim attached to the narrower concept is not, because the moving piece is not free. That separation is what makes this a false-positive case about a LABEL rather than about a move: refusing the label costs the explanation nothing, because the concept that is true is reported beside it. Five of the 788 shipped puzzles carry a discovered check the defender can answer without moving the king.

cases.surface_pattern: A knight on d4 stands between a rook on d1 and the enemy king on d8, and Ne6+ gives check from e6 while stepping off the d-file. That is the double-check geometry, and it is the exact shape of this record's own positive example.
cases.why_not: A black bishop stands on d6. The rook's line is blocked further along, so moving the knight uncovers nothing and the check is a single one. The `discovered-attack` record states this as an indicator_against — "the revealed line is blocked by another unit further along" — and it applies to every concept that reads a battery.
cases.resolution: The API does not report a double check. It reports `pin` — correctly, because the bishop on d6 that blocks the rook is itself pinned against the king — and `discovered-attack`. One black bishop, added to this record's positive example, turns a double check into a pin and nothing else. Syzygy: PROVEN WIN, dtz 3, mate in 19, and the tablebase's best move is Nf5 rather than the checking Ne6. The position is still winning and the concept is still absent, which is the distinction this case exists to hold.

cases.surface_pattern: A black rook on d8 defends the knight on d5 down the file, the black king is boxed in on the back rank, and White has rooks on d1 and e1. Every piece of the overloading picture is on the board, and it is this record's positive example with one man added.
cases.why_not: The one man added is a second black rook, on e8. Overloading is a claim that ONE piece is asked to do two jobs at once; here there are two pieces and two jobs. After Rxd5 Rxd5, the rook on e8 still guards the back rank and there is no mate.
cases.resolution: The API does not report overloading. Stockfish 18 says -4.30 at depth 22 and its first move is Rxe8+, trading into a position where Black is a knight up — so Rxd5, the move that works in the positive example, is simply a blunder here. Read against this record's positive at +6.73: one rook added to the defence and the same move goes from winning a knight to losing one. This record has no matcher, and the reason is on the record — an overload is a claim about being asked to do both at once, which is a property of what the attacker can arrange rather than of what is on the board.

cases.surface_pattern: The bishop on h3 is attacked by the pawn on g4, and it takes it. A piece under attack that grabs something on its way is the picture of a desperado.
cases.why_not: This record's own exception, which it states first: "The whole idea rests on the piece being genuinely unsaveable. Verify that first." The bishop has seven safe squares. Nothing is being sold dearly; a piece that is attacked once and can move is just a piece taking a pawn.
cases.resolution: The API does not report a desperado. This record has no matcher and its limitations say why: 'cannot be saved' is a claim about every legal move the piece has and about what happens after each, which is a search rather than a static test. What a static test WOULD find here is a piece under attack making a capture, which is the surface pattern and is not the concept. Stockfish: 0.00 — the capture is correct and wins nothing, because king and bishop against king is drawn. This record's positive example is a rook that genuinely cannot be saved and is worth 748 centipawns over the alternative; the difference between the two positions is whether the piece had somewhere to go.

cases.surface_pattern: Rook and pawn against rook, the pawn on the sixth, the attacking king in front of it, the defending king directly opposing on the queening file. Every visible ingredient of the Philidor defence is here.
cases.why_not: The defending rook is on the seventh rank, in front of the pawn. Philidor's method is that the rook holds the rank in FRONT of the pawn only until the pawn reaches the sixth, and then drops to the eighth to check from behind. The pawn has reached the sixth and the rook has not dropped back, so the defence is not set up — and by then it is too late to set it up.
cases.resolution: PROVEN WIN in 29, dtz 5, best move Kf6. The API does not report the Philidor position. This is the case this record has been missing: four earlier constructions with the pawon on the fourth rank all came back DRAWN, because there the defence holds from almost anywhere, and that finding is registered as this record's OPEN case. It is a different claim from this one. The open case asks for a position where the third-rank defence FAILS; this one shows a position where the defence is ABSENT and the ending is lost, which establishes that the method is necessary rather than that it is breakable.

cases.surface_pattern: Knight against knight with two kings. By material this is a knight ending, and it is the only kind of position the phrase literally describes.
cases.why_not: Botvinnik's formula is that 'a knight ending is really a pawn ending', and everything this record contains is about how that transfers: the active king, the outside passed pawn, the breakthrough, zugzwang. With no pawns on the board there is no pawn ending for the knight ending to be like, so the concept has no content here rather than being wrong.
cases.resolution: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0. The API reports `opposition` at high confidence — the kings are one square apart in an endgame — and says nothing about knight endings, which is the right pair of answers. The interesting half is what the concept would have to say if it fired: every technique on this record depends on a pawn existing, and a system that reported 'knight ending' here would be naming the material rather than the ending.

cases.surface_pattern: A rook and a knight each, kings on the board, no pawns. Four pieces, two kinds, and an ending that is neither a pure rook ending nor a pure knight ending.
cases.why_not: This record's subject is endings where 'the two sides hold DIFFERENT kinds of material — rook against two minors, queen against rook and pieces, bishop against knight'. Here both sides hold the same kinds. There is no exchange-rate question to get wrong, which is the whole thing the record is about: the point count becomes unreliable exactly where the kinds differ.
cases.resolution: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, best move Nd1. The API reports `open-file` and nothing else. The case is registered because 'mixed' is a word about the RELATION between two armies rather than about how many kinds of piece are present, and a detector counting piece types on a board would get this backwards — it would see two kinds and call the ending mixed, when what makes an ending mixed is the two sides holding different ones.

cases.surface_pattern: A quiet position with no checks, no captures and nothing hanging — exactly the conditions under which this record's principles apply, and the state in which 'improve the piece doing least' is the standard advice.
cases.why_not: There are no pieces. Every white and black man is a pawn or a king, the structure is rammed shut on every file, and no plan of any kind is available to either side. The principles on this record are about choosing between candidate moves in a position with pieces in it; a position with none is quiet in the way an empty room is quiet.
cases.resolution: The API reports nothing at all here, and the same position is registered against `restraint`, `prophylaxis` and `planning` for the same reason — each is a claim about what a move is FOR, and there is nothing for a move to be for. Stockfish 18: 0.00, with both kings walking about on the kingside. Four records now share this board, which makes it the most-reused negative in the base and, for that reason, worth stating plainly: a position where nothing is happening is not evidence that a concept is subtle, it is evidence that the concept needs something to be happening.

cases.surface_pattern: White has four pawns abreast in the centre on c4, d4, e5 and f4 and has spent every move building them. Occupy the centre with pawns is the classical instruction, followed to the letter.
cases.why_not: The doctrine has two halves and this is only the first. Steinitz's other half is TIMING — you may attack, or commit, only when you have earned the right — and White has developed one piece. This record's own definition says both halves 'are still the base of the game'; a pawn centre built ahead of the pieces is the first half practised without the second.
cases.resolution: Letelier-Fischer, Leipzig 1960. The API reports `center-control` for White — which is true, White does control more of it — and does not report the classical school, which has no matcher and should not. Stockfish 18 at depth 24: -0.10, level, with the centre complete and nothing gained; Fischer answered with ...d6 and ...f6 and won in twenty-three. The annotation names the mechanism: 'when central pawns are not supported by pieces, they can become an easy target'. The same position is `historical-principles`' positive example, a rule caught losing its condition, and `pawn-storm`'s counterexample.

cases.surface_pattern: Both sides have fianchettoed. Bishops on g2 and g7 on the long diagonals, knights on f3 and f6, no pawn on e4 or e5 — the hypermodern picture, twice.
cases.why_not: The ground principle is to control the centre INDIRECTLY with pieces, inviting the opponent to occupy it so the pawns become targets. Neither bishop bears on anything: g2 is blocked by its own knight on f3 and by the d4 pawn beyond it, g7 by its own knight on f6 and the d5 pawn. Nobody is being invited to occupy anything, and the centre is already symmetrically fixed.
cases.resolution: The API reports nothing here at all. +0.27 at depth 22, settled at depth 21 — an ordinary symmetrical position. The case is registered because the fianchetto is the most recognisable thing about the school and is the part that carries none of the content: this record's positive example, Reti-Capablanca after 8.d3, has White's bishop on b2 bearing down an OPEN long diagonal at a centre Black is about to occupy. The picture is nearly the same and the idea is absent.

cases.surface_pattern: A piece sacrificed in the opening for a big centre and fast development, with every white piece pointing at the black king. A willingness to give material for the initiative is the first thing Britannica lists about this school.
cases.why_not: Britannica lists four features and this position has one of them wearing the others' clothes. The Halloween Gambit is not prepared, not sound, and not a considered appreciation of material — it is a piece for two tempi. This record's positive example is a world-championship game opening with a thirty-year-old published recommendation of Alekhine's, which is what the school's word for preparation means.
cases.resolution: The API reports `center-control` and `blockade` and says nothing about any school. Stockfish 18 at depth 22: +1.71 from Black's side — the same figure the `compensation` record quotes for this position and the same one that record's trap names, 'the Halloween Gambit position has active pieces and measures 1.75 pawns worse'. Activity, material given, an initiative of a kind, and none of it is the thing the school is named for.

cases.surface_pattern: A concrete position with an extra bishop and an extra pawn, exactly the kind of material edge modern play is supposed to convert by calculation rather than by rule.
cases.why_not: No amount of calculation changes it. The bishop is the wrong colour for the h-pawn's queening square and the defending king cannot be driven from the corner by any series of moves. This record's thesis is that concrete analysis has displaced principle; here principle — one sentence about bishop colour — settles the position and analysis adds nothing to it.
cases.resolution: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, over every legal continuation. The API reports `wrong-rook-pawn` at high confidence, which is the sentence that decides it, and says nothing about calculation. Worth keeping beside this: Stockfish 18 at depth 26 evaluates the same position at +0.92 — the engine, which is the instrument the modern school is built on, is WRONG here and the old rule is right. That is the sharpest available counterweight to this record's own thesis, and it is why the record is filed as a historical-teaching-principle rather than as a fact.

cases.surface_pattern: The Lucena position — a rule taught since the fifteenth century, stated without conditions, and repeated in every endgame book since. Exactly the profile of a principle this record collects.
cases.why_not: This record collects principles that have been QUALIFIED, reattributed or disproved, and its own definition names the three fates: losing a condition, losing its author, or being shown false. The Lucena rule has suffered none of them. It is not a rule of thumb at all — it is a proven result, and it is filed in this base as a `named-theoretical-position` for that reason.
cases.resolution: PROVEN WIN, dtz 15, mate in 41, and the tablebase's own first move is Rd1+ — the first check of the bridge. The API reports `passed-pawn`, `king-activation` and `open-file` and nothing historical. The case exists because this record's subject is the HISTORY of a claim rather than its content, and history is not on a board: what distinguishes a rule that needed qualifying from one that did not is a fact about the literature, and no position can carry it. That is also why the record's detectability is recorded as mechanical only for the narrow purpose of matching named principles by text.

cases.surface_pattern: A queen ending with a passed pawn. This record's headline claim is that in queen endings 'an advanced passed pawn outweighs extra material' and that 'how far advanced a passer is matters more than how many pawns each side has'.
cases.why_not: The claim has 'advanced' in it and the pawn is on the third rank. The mechanism the record describes is that a queen can escort a passer to promotion alone, without the king; a pawn five squares from queening gives the defending queen five moves to arrange checks, and the material count decides after all.
cases.resolution: PROVEN LOSS for the side with the passer, dtz -9, mate in 20 against. The API reports `passed-pawn` and `king-activation` and says nothing about queen endings, which have no matcher. What makes the case worth registering is that the record's own sentence contains the condition and the condition is the whole claim: read without the word 'advanced', the sentence says a passed pawn beats a queen, and this position is what that would mean.

cases.surface_pattern: Both sides have two rooks and pawns. Rooks are the most common piece to reach an ending with, and this record is 'the most common and least rule-governed endings'.
cases.why_not: Both sides also have a bishop, and every principle on this record is about what rooks do when there is nothing else — an active rook makes threats and goes where it likes, a passive one is chained to a pawn, and giving a pawn to activate a rook is routinely correct. None of that survives a minor piece being on the board to defend with and to trade against.
cases.resolution: The API reports `opposite-coloured-bishops` — which is the concept that DOES apply here — and nothing about rook endings. +0.12 at depth 20 in a symmetric position. The case is registered because 'rook ending' is a claim about what is left rather than about what is present, and a detector reading the piece list would find two rooks each and stop there.

cases.surface_pattern: An ordinary middlegame with pieces developed, a queen on d4, bishops on b2 and d5, and no obvious weakness on either side. A positional evaluation would count the features and report a roughly balanced position with a small pull.
cases.why_not: The position is decided by a single move. Bxb7+ uncovers a check and wins on the spot: +4.67 at depth 22, first choice by nearly four pawns. Nothing in the static features carries that; the concept's method — identify durable features, weigh them, draw a verdict — is the wrong instrument for a position whose answer is one move deep.
cases.resolution: Shipped puzzle mi-f2e1be14e7. The API reports `battery`, `bad-bishop`, `king-safety` and `center-control` — a perfectly reasonable feature scan — and does not claim to have evaluated the position. That separation is the point: this record has no matcher, and the reason on the record is that a positional evaluation is a JUDGEMENT assembled from features rather than a feature, so reporting the features is the honest half of it. This base's ambiguous example for the same record is the opposite failure, Adams-Kasparov, where the features say one thing and the truth is +2.12 the other way.

cases.surface_pattern: Bxh7+ gives up a bishop for a pawn — one advantage, the bishop pair and the extra piece, exchanged for another, an exposed king. Trading one kind of advantage for another is the concept, word for word.
cases.why_not: Nothing is obtained. The record's second trap says a transformation must be for a MORE convertible advantage; here the knight on f6 simply takes on h7 and White has given a piece for a pawn. A transformation that acquires nothing is not a transformation, it is a blunder, and this record's first trap warns of the mirror error — that a real transforming move 'often looks like a concession'.
cases.resolution: The API does not report a transformation. It reports `sacrifice` at medium with the record's caution attached, `pin` and `trapped-piece` — all true of the move, none of them claiming it is good. Stockfish 18: the position is 0.00 with a normal move and Bxh7+ scores -3.89, and the refutation is Nxh7 rather than Kxh7. This record has no matcher and its third trap says why: 'the concept describes a player's INTENTION. This system observes moves, not intentions, and must not attribute a transformation to a move without evidence of what it obtained.'

cases.surface_pattern: The rook on d2 steps aside and the rook on d1 behind it is left with a clear file. Vacating a square so a friendly piece can use the line is the concept, word for word.
cases.why_not: The line arrives nowhere. The d-file dead-ends at White's own pawn on d4, which is rammed against d5 and cannot move. Clearance is 'usually recognised by the moving piece going somewhere pointless or losing itself — the value is entirely in the vacated square', and here the vacated square is worth nothing, so all that is left is the pointless move.
cases.resolution: The API reports `worst-placed-piece` at low confidence — the rook does get more scope on a2 — and nothing about clearance, which has no matcher. The same board is `battery`'s registered false-positive case for the same underlying reason: two line pieces on a file that arrives at their own rammed pawn combine nothing, whether they stay stacked or unstack. Stockfish at depth 26 in that entry plays Ra1, taking the front rook OFF the file, which is the engine agreeing that the file is worthless from the other direction.

cases.surface_pattern: Ra8+ forces the black king to move to h7 — a check that must be answered by a king move to a specific square is exactly how a decoy operates.
cases.why_not: Nothing is waiting on h7. A decoy lures a piece ONTO a square where a tactic works against it — a fork square, a mating square, a line where a pin or skewer becomes available — and White has a rook and three pawns. The king is forced to a square and the square is safe.
cases.resolution: The API reports `open-file` and nothing else; `decoy` has no matcher and this record's limitations say why — the motif is 'only identifiable by looking at the resulting position, so it cannot be detected from the move alone'. This case is the cheap version of that: forcing a king to a square is mechanical and trivial to detect, and it is the half of the concept that carries none of the meaning. The position is dead level.

cases.surface_pattern: Rxd5 attacks the rook on d8 that is defending the knight, and a capture the defender must answer is the standard deflecting device.
cases.why_not: There is a second rook on e8. Deflection removes a defender FROM A DUTY, and the duty here — guarding the back rank — is held by two pieces. This record's second exception says it: 'deflecting a defender that has a second defender behind it achieves nothing.'
cases.resolution: The API does not report deflection, which has no matcher at all — `themesOf()` refuses to claim it, because every cheap test for it fires where it is not true. Stockfish 18: -4.30 at depth 22, and its first move is Rxe8+ rather than Rxd5. The same board is `overloading`'s registered false-positive case, and the two records fail on it for one reason said two ways: overloading needs one piece with two duties, deflection needs a duty that ends when the piece leaves, and a spare defender destroys both.

cases.surface_pattern: Nd6 puts a piece on the line between the rook on d8 and the knight it defends on d5. Blocking a defender's line is the definition of interference.
cases.why_not: The rook takes it. An interference has to be an obstruction the defender cannot remove, or one whose removal costs more than the target; a knight dropped on a square the defending rook covers is neither. The concept's whole content is that the line stays blocked.
cases.resolution: The API reports `hanging-piece` at high confidence — which is exactly right about the knight on d6 — and nothing about interference. The numbers make the case sharper than a description could: with a normal move the position is +4.22 for White, because Ne3 attacks the knight on d5 a second time and wins it; the interfering Nd6 scores -4.20. Eight and a half pawns thrown away by a move that satisfies the concept's surface description.

cases.surface_pattern: The queen on d5 attacks the rook on a8 down the long diagonal and the pawn on f7 down the other. Two enemy units attacked at once by one piece, which is this record's precondition exactly.
cases.why_not: The precondition has a second half: 'two distinct threats that CANNOT BOTH BE MET'. Both can. The rook on a8 is defended by the rook on b8 and the pawn on f7 by the king, and a queen taking a defended rook or a defended pawn is not a threat at all — nothing needs answering, so there is nothing for one move to fail to answer.
cases.resolution: The API does not report a double attack. Stockfish 18 at depth 22 says -4.90 for the side making it and retreats the queen to d1. This is the geometric half of the concept without the arithmetic half, and it is the commonest way a reader gets the motif wrong: counting how many enemy pieces a queen touches is easy and says nothing, and what makes the difference is whether taking either one is worth doing.
